docs.title: ProbeOwl
docs.text:
ProbeOwl validates production data across databases and APIs, safely. When a customer says their top-up never arrived, or a visitor's card still opens doors it shouldn't, you type one ID and ProbeOwl looks everywhere that subject's data lives: tables in SQL Server, Oracle and MariaDB, and REST APIs. Then it shows you what it found, what's missing and which rule broke, with the exact query behind every answer.

It runs on your own machine. It reads only from replicas in Production, never writes, and every lookup goes through guards: one SELECT, a row cap, timeouts, and masked personal data.

There are two ways to look:

  • Inspect shows a subject's current state: a visitor and every card they hold.
  • Validate checks that a flow ran correctly: a top-up was captured, confirmed by webhook and posted to the ledger once.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• Getting started: run the examples, with their planted problems, in one command.
  • Your first application: owl init, then your own connector, entity and probe.
  • Concepts: applications, connectors, entities, locations, probes and outcomes, on one worked example.
  • Safety: every refusal, what it protects, and what to do.

The CLI reference lists every owl command, and Troubleshooting covers the problems people meet on their first run.

docs.title: CLI reference
docs.text:
owl is ProbeOwl's command line, installed with uv tool install probeowl. From a source checkout, run it as uv run owl ... in backend/.

owl serve is ProbeOwl itself: it loads the config folder, holds the guards and runs every probe. owl validate, owl inspect, owl catalog import, owl kill and owl reload are its clients, like the web app, so a run from the command line is checked, limited and audited exactly like one from the browser. Start owl serve first. They find it at $PROBEOWL_SERVER, else http://127.0.0.1:7878, or wherever --server says. They take no --config.

owl init, owl connector add, owl check, owl store and owl runbook hash read the config folder or the store themselves, and need nothing running.

Command What it does Needs running owl init Writes a config folder for a first application and connector, step by step Nothing owl connector add Adds a connector to an application, or bindings for the environments one lacks Nothing owl serve Serves ProbeOwl on 127.0.0.1: the web app at /, this guide at /guide/, the API under /api The store (owl store init) owl check <folder> Checks every YAML file, the references between them, and every lookup Nothing owl validate <entity> <value> Runs an entity's validate probe on one subject owl serve owl inspect <value> Runs an inspect probe on a subject owl serve owl catalog import <connector> Imports a SQL connector's schema: tables, columns, keys, indexes, row estimates; never data owl serve owl kill on, off, list Turns kill switches on and off, and lists those on owl serve owl reload Makes owl serve load its config folder again, without a restart owl serve owl store init, upgrade Creates or upgrades ProbeOwl's own store Nothing owl store ddl --dialect <name> Prints the SQL that creates the store, for a DBA to run Nothing owl runbook hash <file> Prints each read query's sql_sha256, for its reviewed block Nothing

docs.title: Common options
docs.text: Option On Meaning --env <name> validate, inspect, catalog import The environment, such as prod or uat. Required --reason <reason> validate, inspect Why: incident, customer_complaint, deploy_verification, audit_or_compliance or proactive_check. Required --reference <text> validate, inspect, kill A Jira key, support case or change ID. Required in Production for runs --notes <text> validate, inspect Free text, kept with the run --application <name> validate, inspect, catalog import, kill Which application, when it isn't clear (required for catalog import) --probe <name> validate, inspect Which probe, when the entity has several --server <url> every client Where owl serve is. Default: $PROBEOWL_SERVER, else http://127.0.0.1:7878 --timeout <seconds> validate, inspect How long to follow the run (default 120) --url <url> serve, store The store's SQLAlchemy URL. Default: $PROBEOWL_STORE_URL, else ~/.probeowl/store.db. Use the variable for a URL with a password

docs.title: owl init
docs.text: Asks for the application, its environments and a first connector with a binding per environment, then writes the folder and saves each password in your keychain. Then it offers to test the connections, create the store and import the schema. See Your first application.

docs.title: owl connector add
docs.text:
owl connector add --config probeowl --application wallet

Adds a connector to an application, or, given an existing connector's id, bindings for the environments it isn't bound in yet. It asks the same questions as owl init, with the connector's existing binding as the defaults, and you choose which environments to bind. Each password goes to your keychain, never to a file.

It writes one file: the new connector's, or the existing one with the new bindings added and its comments kept. If the folder wouldn't load with that file, the change is undone and nothing is saved. With a store, the change is recorded in the audit. Then it offers to test the new bindings and, for a SQL connector, to import its schema.

Option Default Meaning --config <folder> $PROBEOWL_CONFIG, else the current folder The config folder: the one owl serve was started with --application <name> Asked, when the folder holds several The application to add to

It works on a folder owl serve refuses because a probe needs a binding that isn't there, which is how you add that binding. If others are still missing afterwards, it lists them. Then owl reload loads the change into owl serve.

docs.title: owl serve
docs.text:
owl serve --config probeowl
Option Default Meaning --config <folder> $PROBEOWL_CONFIG, else the current folder The applications to load --port <n> 7878 The port on 127.0.0.1 --url <url> $PROBEOWL_STORE_URL, else ~/.probeowl/store.db The store --web-origin <url> $PROBEOWL_WEB_ORIGINS Where else the web app is served from, on loopback only. Vite on 5173 and 4173 is always accepted. Repeat for several --log-file <path> ~/.probeowl/owl-serve.log The log, readable only by you --debug-driver-errors off Log the drivers' raw error text, which can hold values from statements and personal data

It refuses to start if the folder has errors (run owl check to see them all) or the store isn't at this release (run owl store upgrade).

docs.title: owl check
docs.text:
owl check probeowl
owl check probeowl --no-connect

Checks the YAML against its schema, the references between files, and every lookup against the save checks that need no database. For Production SQL bindings, it also asks whether the login can read plans, and warns with the grant if not. --no-connect skips that. Exit code 1 when anything is wrong.

docs.title: owl validate and owl inspect
docs.text:
owl validate topup tp_91f2c7 --env uat --reason incident
owl validate topup pay_7hq2m9 --env prod --reason customer_complaint --reference SUP-20931
owl inspect C204518 --env prod --reason customer_complaint --reference SUP-20931

Any identifier of the subject works: ProbeOwl recognises it by its pattern, or use --identifier on owl inspect. The CLI prints each location as it's read, then each expectation, then the run's status. Exit codes:

Code Meaning 0 Passed 1 Failed, or skipped (a paused connector, a kill switch) 2 Not run: refused before it started, or owl serve couldn't be reached or followed 3 Ambiguous (inspect): the value matched several subjects, and nothing else ran

The run header names the probe by its title, then its id: Run 9305b99c-...: Top-up completed (wallet/topup_completed) on tp_91f2c7 in uat.

docs.title: owl catalog import
docs.text:
owl catalog import wallet_db --application wallet --env uat

Reads the schema, never data, and stores it. The Tables screen then suggests a label for each table.

docs.title: owl kill
docs.text:
owl kill on --all --reason "replica on fire"
owl kill on --application wallet --reason "wallet incident"
owl kill on --application wallet --connector ledger_db --reason "ledger failover"
owl kill list
owl kill off --all --reason "resolved" --reference INC-1042

--all is the global switch, asked for by name. A connector switch covers that connector in every environment. Turning one off leaves broader switches that are on in place. See Safety.

docs.title: owl reload
docs.text:
owl reload

Makes owl serve read its config folder again and load it, as it does at start, so added or changed connectors, bindings, entities and probes are loaded without a restart. It prints what it loaded and which applications and connectors changed, and is recorded in the audit. The Reload configuration button on the Connectors screen does the same. Screens already open in the browser read again within about 15 seconds, or at their next request, and say so; a draft in the Probe editor is kept and checked again against what was loaded.

If owl serve would refuse the folder at start, nothing changes and the first error is shown (owl check <folder> lists them all). It's refused while a run is running. Kill switches stay as they are. Plugins, the port, the store and the log file change only with a restart.

docs.title: owl store
docs.text:
owl store init                                  # create, or upgrade to this release
owl store upgrade
owl store ddl --dialect postgresql > store.sql  # for a DBA: sqlite, postgresql, mssql, oracle, mariadb

The store holds runs, the audit, schema imports and kill switches. It's never a probed database. SQLite on a network share loses writes when several people use it, so owl store init refuses one: use a server database for a team store.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: One example runs through this page. A contractor reports a lost card, C204518. Support needs to know: whose card is it, which other cards does that person hold, and does the door controller agree with the database about each one?

docs.title: Application and environment
docs.text:
An application is a product area, such as Wallet or Card access. It owns its connectors, entities, probes, runbooks and table catalog, and you choose it in the top bar. Each application has environments, such as Production and UAT. Production has the strictest rules: replicas only, guards that can't be relaxed, and a reason and reference on every run.

The card belongs to the Card access application, in Production.

docs.title: Connector, binding and role
docs.text:
A connector is a read-only client for one system: access_db for the MariaDB database, door_controller_api for the controller's REST API. A binding says where a connector points in one environment: host, database, login and the keychain entry holding its password. A connector with no binding in an environment is Not configured there.

A Production binding's role says what kind of copy it reads: a read replica, a readable secondary or an Active Data Guard standby. The Connectors screen shows it under the connector's name.

docs.title: Entity, subject, identifiers and root key
docs.text:
An entity is a kind of business subject: a top-up, a visitor. A subject is one of them: visitor VP00012931.

An identifier is any value that can find a subject. A visitor has four: the profile id, a card id, an employee number and an email. Each says whether it is unique, and may have a pattern, so ProbeOwl can tell which one you typed: C204518 matches ^C\d{6}$, so it's a card id. One identifier is the root key, visitor_profile_id: every other lookup starts from it.

To get from the card to the visitor, the card id is looked up in the cards location, which gives the visitor's profile id. If an identifier finds more than one subject, as a shared email can, the run is Ambiguous and lists the matches. You pick one, or run them all.

docs.title: Locations, key graph and cardinality
docs.text:
A location is one place a subject's data lives, with its own lookup:

locations:
  profile:
    using: access_db
    lookup: SELECT ... FROM visitor_profile WHERE id = :visitor_profile_id
  cards:
    using: access_db
    lookup: SELECT ... FROM cards WHERE visitor_profile_id = :visitor_profile_id
    cardinality: many
    each:
      controller:
        using: door_controller_api
        lookup: GET /cards/{{card_id}}
        max_fanout: 10

The key graph says where each location gets its key. By default it's the root key. key_from: record.provider_payment_id takes it from another location's field instead, so locations are read in order, and those that can run together do.

Cardinality says how many records to expect: one (the default), optional or many. More records than that is Ambiguous. A many location returns at most its max_rows, and never more than the connector's row ceiling.

docs.title: Fan-out
docs.text: each: repeats a lookup for each row of a many location: here, the door controller is asked about every card. That's fan-out. It's capped by max_fanout, so a visitor with 500 cards doesn't become 500 API calls. Rows past the cap are not checked, and any check that needed them is skipped and says so.

docs.title: Probe kinds
docs.text:
A probe is a saved, reviewed check: the locations to read and the expectations to test.

  • Inspect shows a subject's current state: the visitor and every card.
  • Validate checks that a flow ran correctly: a top-up was captured, confirmed and posted.
  • Health will run on a schedule across an application to find stuck records (phase 2).

docs.title: Expectations
docs.text:
An expectation is one rule in a probe:

expect:
  - count(cards where status == 'active') <= 1
  - all(cards where status == 'active', valid_to > now())
  - all(cards, controller.status == status)

Each passes, fails or is skipped. A condition, when:, applies a step's expectations only in some states, such as when: record.status == 'failed'.

Missing data never passes a check. A location that is Missing has no record, so only counting reads it: count(), exists() and none() see no rows. Anything else that reads it is skipped, with "needs ledger, which is Missing": sum, min, max, all, any, unique, or a field such as payment.amount. A skip fails the run, because a run can't pass on data it couldn't see. Without this rule, sum(credit) == sum(debit) would pass as 0 == 0 on a ledger that isn't there. For a location that may be absent, start the step with when: exists(refund).

A filter that leaves no rows of a Found location is different. all(cards where status == 'active', ...) still holds for a visitor whose cards are all revoked: the rule is about the location, not the filter.

docs.title: Outcomes
docs.text:
Each location ends with one outcome:

Outcome Meaning Found The lookup returned its record or records. Missing The lookup worked and returned nothing. Waiting Not found yet, but still inside its window (within). Blocked Its key could not be found, because an earlier location failed or a link was empty. Ambiguous More records than its cardinality allows. Error The lookup itself failed: refused, timed out or unreachable. The reason is in the evidence. Stale The replica is further behind than the window, so "missing" can't be trusted. Not configured The connector has no binding in this environment.

Blocked is not Missing. A top-up whose ledger_txn_id was never saved can't be looked up in the ledger at all, and ProbeOwl reports the empty link itself as the finding.

docs.title: Caveats and replica lag
docs.text: ProbeOwl reads Production from replicas, which can be behind. When it knows the lag, and the lag is longer than a location's window, a Missing becomes Stale. When it can't read the lag (the login lacks the grant; see Connectors), a Missing in Production carries a caveat: "replica lag unknown, the record may not have arrived yet". So does every expectation that read it, and the run.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text: Every outcome has its evidence: the exact query that ran, its parameters, the guards applied, and the raw rows, with personal data masked. If you doubt a result, the evidence shows exactly what was asked and what came back.

docs.title: Run and investigation
docs.text:
A run is one execution of a probe on one subject. Everything is stored: every lookup, every result and how long it took. A run you start is an investigation, with its record: a reason (always) and a reference such as a Jira key (in Production), plus optional notes.

For C204518, the run finds visitor VP00012931 with three cards and fails three expectations: two active cards, one active card past its end date, and a revoked card the controller still reports as active.

docs.title: Connectors
docs.text: A connector is a read-only client for one system: a SQL Server, Oracle or MariaDB database, or a REST API. It has one binding per environment, saying where it points there.

docs.title: Adding a connector
docs.text:
owl init writes your first connector. For the next ones, run this in your config folder, the one owl serve was started with:

owl connector add --application wallet

It asks for the connector's type and a binding per environment, keeps each password in your keychain, and checks the folder still loads before it keeps the file. Given an existing connector's id, it adds bindings for the environments that connector lacks. See the CLI reference.

Or write the file yourself, in the application's connectors/ folder:

# wallet/connectors/ledger_db.yaml
connector: ledger_db
type: oracle                 # sqlserver, oracle, mariadb or rest
owner: payments-team
guards:
  row_ceiling: 1000          # the most rows any lookup on it can return
environments:
  prod:
    host: ledger-standby.internal
    port: 1521
    database: LEDGERPDB      # Oracle: the service name
    schema: LEDGER           # Oracle only: where unqualified table names resolve
    user: probeowl_ro
    secret: keyring:probeowl/ledger_db.prod
    replica: true            # an Active Data Guard standby
  uat:
    host: ledger-uat.internal
    port: 1521
    database: LEDGERPDB
    schema: LEDGER_UAT
    user: probeowl_ro
    secret: keyring:probeowl/ledger_db.uat

Then save each password in your system keychain, under the name its secret gives:

uvx keyring set probeowl ledger_db.prod

A secret is a reference, never the password itself: keyring:<service>/<name> reads the system keychain, and env:<VARIABLE> reads an environment variable. ProbeOwl won't read a keyring that keeps secrets in files rather than in your operating system's keychain.

Then load it into owl serve: Reload configuration on the Connectors screen, or owl reload. Check the connector there with Test connection. owl check <folder> checks the files without starting anything.

A connector with no binding in an environment is Not configured there: probes that need it can't run in that environment, and owl check says so.

docs.title: Binding settings
docs.text:
Setting For Meaning host, port SQL Where the database listens database SQL The database (SQL Server, MariaDB) or service name (Oracle) schema Oracle The schema unqualified table names resolve in user, secret SQL The read-only login, and where its password is replica SQL This binding reads a replica. Production bindings must max_replica_lag SQL Past this lag (default 60s), the circuit breaker pauses the connector allowed_databases SQL Server, MariaDB Other databases on the same server that lookups may name encrypt, encrypt_reason MariaDB, Oracle TLS is on unless you turn it off and say why. SQL Server always encrypts trust_server_certificate, ..._reason SQL Accept any server certificate, with a reason, as for a local test container time_zone Oracle Each session's time zone, as an offset; default: the database's own base_url, secret REST The API's address, and its token if it needs one

owl check refuses a Production binding that isn't a replica, and one that turns off TLS or trusts any certificate without a reason.

docs.title: What the login needs
docs.text:
A probe login reads, and nothing else. Ask your DBA for a login with:

Database To read For the index check at save time SQL Server db_datareader, or SELECT on the tables probes read GRANT SHOWPLAN TO <login> in the database MariaDB SELECT on the tables probes read Nothing more: EXPLAIN needs only SELECT Oracle SELECT on the tables probes read Write access to PLAN_TABLE (public by default; a read-only standby has none)

SHOWPLAN shows plans; it doesn't let the login run anything else or read more data. Without the plan grant, saving a probe for Production needs your acknowledgement that its plan couldn't be checked, recorded with your name, and owl check warns and names the grant.

docs.title: Replica lag
docs.text:
Before a run's first lookup on a replica, ProbeOwl reads how far it is behind its primary. This needs one more grant. It's optional, but without it lag is always unknown:

Database Grant SQL Server 2022 and later GRANT VIEW DATABASE PERFORMANCE STATE TO <login>; in the database MariaDB 10.5.9 and later GRANT REPLICA MONITOR ON *.* TO '<login>'@'<host>'; (same as SLAVE MONITOR) Oracle GRANT SELECT ON SYS.V_$DATAGUARD_STATS TO <login>;

Without it:

  • the Connectors screen and each run's evidence say replica lag unknown: missing <grant>;
  • the circuit breaker can't pause the connector for lag;
  • a location is never Stale, so a record that hasn't reached the replica yet shows as Missing, with a caveat in Production.

docs.title: Runbook steps on Oracle's v$ views
docs.text: A runbook read step on a dynamic performance view, such as v$session, needs SELECT on the view itself: GRANT SELECT ON SYS.V_$SESSION TO <login>;. Without it, the step is copy only, and says which grant is missing.

docs.title: Time offsets
docs.text: ProbeOwl never compares a time that has an offset (SQL Server datetimeoffset, Oracle TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE) with a column that has none, because the database would read one of them in a time zone it guesses, and match rows hours off. Saving refuses such a lookup unless the SQL converts the value, for example CAST(:at AS datetime2), and names the conversions that work. A run refuses a typed time with an offset against a column without one, and the other way round. These checks use the column types from the latest schema import.

docs.title: Test connection
docs.text: The Connectors screen shows each connector's health, role, replica lag and plan access in the chosen environment. Test connection connects once, now, and says how long it took or why it failed, as a fixed message that never contains hosts, logins or passwords.

docs.title: Your first application
docs.text: This page sets ProbeOwl up for one of your own systems: an application, its environments and a first connector, then an entity and a probe. It assumes ProbeOwl is installed, as in Getting started.

docs.title: 1. Run owl init
docs.text:
owl init

owl init asks its questions first, and writes nothing until you have answered all of them. If you stop part-way, nothing is left behind.

This writes a config folder and saves passwords in your system keychain, never in a file.
Config folder [./probeowl]:
Application id, such as wallet or card_access: wallet
Application title [Wallet]:
Owning team: payments-team
Environments, comma-separated [prod,uat]:
  Which one is Production? (none if none is) [prod]:
  Title for prod [Production]:
  Title for uat [UAT]:

First connector
Type (sqlserver, oracle, mariadb, rest) [sqlserver]:
Connector id [wallet_sqlserver]: wallet_db
  Binding for prod (Production)
    Host [127.0.0.1]: wallet-replica.internal
    Port [1433]:
    Database [wallet]:
    Read-only login: probeowl_ro
    Password (hidden; saved to the keychain as probeowl/wallet_db.prod):
    Is this a read replica, readable secondary or Active Data Guard standby? [y/N]: y
    Trust the server certificate without checking it? [y/N]:
  Binding for uat (UAT)
    ...

What to know about the questions:

  • Ids (wallet, wallet_db) use a-z, 0-9 and _. They become file names and appear in lookups, so owl init asks again for anything else. The application id has no default: choose the product area's own name. An application spans its environments, so an id with an environment's word in it, such as access_uat_test, is offered again without it (access). The connector id suggested is the application and the database type, such as wallet_sqlserver; naming it after the system, such as wallet_db, reads better.
  • Production must be a replica. ProbeOwl reads Production only from a read replica, readable secondary or Active Data Guard standby, never from the primary. If you answer no, owl init stops and writes nothing: ask your DBA for one, then run it again.
  • The login is read-only. The Connectors page lists what it needs on each database.
  • Passwords go into your system keychain, as probeowl/<connector>.<environment>. The files refer to them, and never contain them. On a machine whose only keyring keeps secrets in files, owl init refuses before the first question.
  • TLS: MariaDB and Oracle connections are encrypted unless you say no and give a reason. SQL Server connections are always encrypted. Trusting a certificate without checking it needs a reason too.
  • Later environments offer the earlier one's answers as defaults. Enter at the password prompt reuses the earlier password.

Then it asks about the store, before it writes anything: Create the store, ProbeOwl's own database for runs and audit, at ~/.probeowl/store.db, or $PROBEOWL_STORE_URL. With it, the setup itself is recorded in the audit: if that can't be recorded, nothing is written and no password is kept. Without it, the setup carries on and says it was not recorded; owl store init creates the store later.

Then it offers two things:

  1. Test the connections, binding by binding: prod: reached in 42 ms, or why not. A binding that isn't reached doesn't stop the setup. Fix it in its file and test it again from the Connectors screen.
  2. Import the connector's schema in your first non-Production environment. It reads tables, columns and indexes, never data, so the Tables screen can list them with a suggested label for each. If you skip it, or it fails, the next steps say how to import later: Import from replica on the Tables screen, or owl catalog import while owl serve runs.

It writes two files:

probeowl/wallet/application.yaml
probeowl/wallet/connectors/wallet_db.yaml

# probeowl/wallet/connectors/wallet_db.yaml
connector: wallet_db
type: sqlserver
owner: payments-team
guards:
  row_ceiling: 1000
environments:
  prod:
    host: wallet-replica.internal
    port: 1433
    database: wallet
    user: probeowl_ro
    secret: keyring:probeowl/wallet_db.prod
    replica: true
  uat:
    ...

docs.title: 2. Start owl serve
docs.text:
owl serve --config probeowl

Open http://127.0.0.1:7878: owl serve serves the web app itself. The application is in the top bar, with its environments.

docs.title: 3. Confirm the table labels
docs.text: Open Tables. Each table the import found has a suggested label, such as Transaction, Master, Log or Audit, and the columns that matter: keys, time, status, links and personal data. Confirm or correct each one. ProbeOwl writes your answers to catalog.yaml in the application's folder. The labels set defaults, and personal-data columns are masked everywhere.

docs.title: 4. Write an entity
docs.text:
An entity says what a subject is and where its data lives. The quickest way is New entity… in the Probe editor: pick the root table from the imported schema and follow its keys to other tables, then check and create it. See New entity.

Or write it yourself. Create probeowl/wallet/entities/topup.yaml:

entity: topup
title: Top-up
root_key: topup_id
owner: payments-team

identifiers:
  topup_id: { pattern: '^tp_[0-9a-z]{6}$', unique: true }

locations:
  record:
    title: Top-up record
    using: wallet_db
    lookup: >
      SELECT id AS topup_id, amount, currency, status, created_at
      FROM topups WHERE id = :topup_id
    exposes: [topup_id, amount, currency, status, created_at]

Every lookup is a single SELECT, with its keys as :parameters, never pasted into the text. Writing probes adds more locations and the key graph that links them.

docs.title: 5. Write a probe, and run it
docs.text:
Open the Probe editor, choose the entity, and start a new probe:

probe: topup_completed
title: Top-up completed
kind: validate
entity: topup
owner: payments-team
expect:
  - record.status in ['succeeded', 'failed', 'pending']

Saving runs the save checks and shows you the change before writing it. Then run it from Validate with a real ID, or test-run the draft before you save.

Check the whole folder at any time:

owl check probeowl

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
You need uv. The web app comes in the package, so nothing else:

uv tool install probeowl
uv tool update-shell

uv tool update-shell adds uv's tool folder to your PATH, once per machine. Open a new terminal after it, then check:

owl --version

If a new terminal says owl isn't found, run uv tool update-shell again and open another one.

Then Your first application sets it up for one of your own systems. To see what it does first, try the examples.

docs.title: The examples
docs.text:
ProbeOwl comes with two example applications. Their test data has problems planted in it on purpose, so you can see what ProbeOwl reports before pointing it at anything of yours:

  • Wallet: top-ups, read from SQL Server, Oracle and a payments API.
  • Card access: visitors and their cards, read from MariaDB and a door controller API.

The examples run from a source checkout. You need uv, Node.js, and for the example databases, either Docker or the native install described below.

git clone https://github.com/saadzarook/probeowl.git
cd probeowl

docs.title: With Docker
docs.text:
bash dev/try.sh --docker

This one command:

  1. Starts the example databases and the two fake APIs with Docker Compose. The first start pulls the images, and Oracle takes a few minutes to seed.
  2. Copies examples/ to ~/.probeowl/try. The examples' passwords go into your system keychain under probeowl-try/, so they can never overwrite an entry a real connector uses.
  3. Gives the copy its own store, and starts owl serve and the web app.

Open http://127.0.0.1:5173 when it says it's up. Ctrl-C stops everything it started. Add --reseed to start the planted data afresh: some card dates are relative to the day the data was seeded.

docs.title: With native databases
docs.text:
If you installed SQL Server, MariaDB and Oracle on your machine with dev/native/ (see its README), use:

bash dev/try.sh --native

Oracle runs in WSL and stops when nothing uses it. Keep it running in a window of its own with bash dev/native/oracle_awake.sh.

docs.title: Ports
docs.text: try.sh uses 7878 for owl serve and 5173 for the web app, and refuses to start if either is taken. Choose others with --api-port and --web-port.

docs.title: What to try
docs.text:
Where Enter What you should see Validate, Wallet, UAT tp_91f2c7 Failed: the ledger entries are Missing, though the payment was captured Validate, Wallet, UAT tp_91f2b9 Passed: every location Found Validate, Wallet, UAT tp_93b001 Failed: the ledger is Blocked, because the top-up never saved its ledger link Inspect, Card access C204518 Three card issues for visitor VP00012931 Inspect, Card access a.rahman@example.com Ambiguous: the email belongs to two visitors

In Production, every run needs a reason and a reference, as it would for real.

From another terminal, the same through the command line:

cd backend
uv run owl validate topup tp_91f2c7 --env uat --reason incident

docs.title: Without databases: mocks only
docs.text:
To see every screen without any database, run the web app against its built-in mocks:

cd web
npm ci
VITE_MOCK_API=true npm run dev

Nothing here talks to owl serve: the answers are fixed, and match the examples.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Your first application sets ProbeOwl up for one of your own systems.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: ProbeOwl holds read access to Production systems, so it is built to refuse first. This page lists each refusal, what it protects, and what to do about it.

docs.title: Read-only, always
docs.text:
Every lookup is a single SELECT. A lookup is parsed when it's saved and again before it runs. Anything else is refused: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DDL, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, lock hints, procedure calls, several statements, or UNION at the top (put it in a subquery). REST connectors send only GET.

What to do: rewrite the lookup as one SELECT. To change data, write a runbook write query: it's stored for a person to copy and run with their own access. ProbeOwl never runs one.

Keys are always bound. :topup_id is a parameter, never text pasted into the SQL, so a pasted ID can't become an injection.

docs.title: Production reads replicas
docs.text:
A Production binding must have replica: true: a read replica, readable secondary or Active Data Guard standby. owl check, owl init and owl serve refuse one that doesn't.

What to do: ask your DBA for a replica binding.

docs.title: Guards on every lookup
docs.text:
Guard What it does If it trips Row cap Each lookup returns at most its location's max_rows, or one row for one and optional, never more than the connector's row ceiling (default 1,000). The cap is added to the query itself (TOP, FETCH FIRST, LIMIT) The result says "showing N of M", and a one location with several rows is Ambiguous Statement timeout 2 seconds per lookup by default That location is Error: "the statement timed out after 2 s" No waiting on locks LOCK_TIMEOUT 0 on SQL Server, short lock waits on MariaDB; Oracle readers never block Error: "a lock was not granted in time" Result size At most 1 MB per lookup Reading stops there, and the result says it was cut short Run time 60 seconds per run; locations not read by then are Error The run says which Concurrency 4 runs at once A new run is refused until one finishes

A failure of one location is that location's Error, with the reason in its evidence. It never crashes the run.

docs.title: Save checks
docs.text:
When a probe is saved, and with owl check for whole folders, ProbeOwl checks each lookup:

  • it's read-only, as above;
  • on a Transaction, Log or Audit table, it filters by a key or a bounded time window, so it never scans a growing table (time filter);
  • its plan seeks an index rather than scanning the table (plan check, which needs the database);
  • PII columns it selects are masked;
  • max_rows is within the row ceiling;
  • times with and without offsets are never compared.

What to do: each failed check says why, and what would pass. A Production login that can't read plans makes the plan check impossible. Then saving needs your explicit acknowledgement, which is recorded with your name. Connectors lists the grant that removes the need.

docs.title: Circuit breaker
docs.text:
Before a run's first lookup on a replica, ProbeOwl reads its lag. If the lag is longer than the binding's max_replica_lag (60 seconds by default), the connector is paused, and runs that need it are Skipped, not failed: "access_db is paused: replica lag 120 s (max 60 s)". The Connectors screen shows the pause and when it ends.

What to do: wait. A replica that far behind would report records as Missing that only haven't arrived yet.

docs.title: Kill switch
docs.text:
A kill switch stops every read at its next lookup: global, for one application, or for one connector. Turning one on or off needs a reason, and is recorded with your name. A banner on every screen says what's stopped and why, and runs are refused while it's on.

owl kill on --application wallet --connector ledger_db --reason "ledger failover in progress"
owl kill list
owl kill off --application wallet --connector ledger_db --reason "failover done"

docs.title: Masking
docs.text: Personal data is masked in the runner, before anything is stored, shown or logged: columns listed in a location's pii, REST fields in its mask, columns the catalog marks as PII, and identifiers marked pii: true. A masked value shows as [masked] on screen, in evidence, in the CLI and in the store. An identifier you typed that is PII, such as an email, is stored masked too.

docs.title: Production investigation record
docs.text: Every run you start records a reason. In Production it also needs a reference: a Jira key, support case or change ID. A Production run without one is refused before it starts. Every run and every change is in the audit, with who, when and where.

docs.title: Local only
docs.text:
owl serve listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Two more checks stop other web pages in your browser from using it:

  • Host check: every request must name owl serve itself, which defeats DNS rebinding.
  • Origin check: every request that changes something must come from the web app's own address and carry ProbeOwl's request header. owl serve accepts its own address and Vite's (127.0.0.1 and localhost, ports 5173 and 4173). For anywhere else on your machine, start it with --web-origin http://127.0.0.1:<port>.

What to do if the web app says owl serve refused it: see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text: Passwords live in your system keychain or in environment variables, never in a file. Bindings hold references (keyring:probeowl/wallet_db.prod). Errors shown on screen or returned by the API are fixed messages, without hosts, logins or passwords. The driver's own error text goes only to the owl serve log, and only with --debug-driver-errors.

docs.title: Probes across several systems
docs.text: A subject's data rarely lives in one place. A visitor's cards are rows in the access database, but whether a door actually opens is up to the door controller, which has its own REST API. This walkthrough builds the probe that checks the two agree, following the card-access example in examples/card-access/.

docs.title: Two connectors
docs.text:
Each system is its own connector, in the application's connectors/ folder:

# card-access/connectors/access_db.yaml
connector: access_db
type: mariadb
owner: access-team
environments:
  prod:
    host: 127.0.0.1
    port: 3306
    database: access
    user: probeowl_ro
    secret: keyring:probeowl/access_db.prod
    replica: true
  uat:
    host: 127.0.0.1
    port: 3306
    database: access_uat
    # ...

# card-access/connectors/door_controller_api.yaml
connector: door_controller_api
type: rest
owner: access-team
environments:
  prod: { base_url: "http://127.0.0.1:8082" }
  uat: { base_url: "http://127.0.0.1:8082" }

owl connector add --application card_access writes a file like these, and keeps each password or token in your keychain. See Connectors.

docs.title: Each location names its connector
docs.text:
The entity lists where a visitor's data lives. Each location reads from exactly one connector, named by using::

# card-access/entities/visitor.yaml
entity: visitor
root_key: visitor_profile_id

locations:
  profile:
    using: access_db
    lookup: >
      SELECT id AS visitor_profile_id, employee_no, email, type, status, created_at
      FROM visitor_profile WHERE id = :visitor_profile_id
    exposes: [visitor_profile_id, employee_no, email, type, status, created_at]
    pii: [email]

  cards:
    using: access_db
    lookup: >
      SELECT card_id, visitor_profile_id, status, valid_from, valid_to, access_group
      FROM cards WHERE visitor_profile_id = :visitor_profile_id
    cardinality: many
    max_rows: 50
    exposes: [card_id, visitor_profile_id, status, valid_from, valid_to, access_group]
    each:
      controller:
        using: door_controller_api
        lookup: GET /cards/{{card_id}}
        max_fanout: 10
        exposes: [status]
        compare: [status]

profile and cards are SQL lookups on access_db: a single SELECT each, with the key as a :name parameter. controller is a REST location on door_controller_api: one GET, with the key in the path as {{name}}. Only GET is ever sent. A REST location's exposes names fields of the JSON it returns, and mask lists any fields holding personal data, which are masked before anything is stored or shown.

docs.title: How the keys flow
docs.text:
A lookup needs a key, and the key graph says where each one comes from:

  1. profile and cards take the root key, visitor_profile_id: the subject you typed, or the one an identifier such as a card ID led to. Neither waits for the other, so they're read together.
  2. controller sits under each:, so it runs once for every row cards returned, with that row's card_id in its path: GET /cards/C204518, then the next card.

A location can also take its key from another location's field with key_from, such as key_from: record.provider_payment_id in the wallet example. It then waits for that location, and if that field is empty it is Blocked: ProbeOwl couldn't look, which is not the same as Missing.

docs.title: Fan-out, and its cap
docs.text:
Repeating a lookup per row is fan-out. It is capped twice, so one subject can never become a flood of calls:

  • max_rows: 50 caps the cards read, never more than access_db's row ceiling.
  • max_fanout: 10 caps the controller calls: a visitor with 30 cards gets 10. Rows past the cap aren't checked, and any expectation that needed them is skipped and says so.

Each controller call has its own outcome and evidence, so one card the controller doesn't know is that card's Missing, not a failed run.

docs.title: The expectation that spans both systems
docs.text:
# card-access/probes/visitor_cards.yaml
probe: visitor_cards
kind: inspect
entity: visitor
expect:
  - count(cards where status == 'active') <= 1
  - all(cards where status == 'active', valid_to > now())
  - all(cards, controller.status == status)     # database and controller agree

The last line checks the two systems agree. Inside all(cards, ...), each card is checked in turn: status is that card's status in the database, and controller.status is what the door controller said about the same card. One card that disagrees fails the expectation, and the result lists the cards that do. The example visitor VP00012931 has three planted problems for you to find.

docs.title: Why there are no joins across databases
docs.text:
There is no SQL that joins access_db to another database, and no lookup reads two connectors at once. Each lookup is one statement, or one GET, on one system, and ProbeOwl matches the results by key itself. That keeps every read small and checkable on its own:

  • it runs under its own connector's guards: the row cap, the statement timeout, no waiting on locks;
  • the save checks, including the plan check, can judge it against its own database;
  • its evidence shows the exact query, parameters and result for that one system;
  • the systems needn't be the same kind of database, or databases at all.

docs.title: Each connector keeps its own guards and kill switch
docs.text:
The limits belong to the connector, not to the probe:

  • access_db has its own row ceiling (guards.row_ceiling, 1,000 by default), and its Production binding reads a replica, paused by the circuit breaker if the replica falls behind.
  • A kill switch can stop one connector without touching the others:
owl kill on --application card_access --connector door_controller_api --reason "controller upgrade"

While it's on, a run that needs the door controller is Skipped: it reads nothing, not even from access_db, and says which switch stopped it. Probes that don't use the controller, and other applications, keep running.

docs.title: When a connector has no binding in an environment
docs.text:
A connector with no binding in an environment is Not configured there, and the Connectors screen says so. In this release, a probe that needs it can't run in that environment at all: owl check, and so owl serve, refuse the folder until you either

  • bind it there: owl connector add --application card_access, then give door_controller_api's id and answer for the missing environment; or
  • leave that environment out of the probe, so it is offered only where every location is bound:
probe: visitor_cards
environments: [prod]

A later release will run the locations it can and show just the unbound one as Not configured.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: The problems people meet on a first run, and how to fix each one.

docs.title: owl isn't found after installing
docs.text:
uv tool install probeowl puts owl in uv's tool folder, which isn't on your PATH until you run:

uv tool update-shell

once, and open a new terminal. uv tool dir --bin shows the folder it adds.

docs.title: The web app shows 422 or 404 errors on first load
docs.text: Fixed in ProbeOwl's first-run work: the Probe editor no longer checks an empty draft, and the Tables screen no longer asks for schemas never imported. If you still see one, update your checkout. A schema never imported is now an empty state with the command to import it.

docs.title: owl serve refuses the web app
docs.text:
The web app says owl serve refused it, or writes such as starting a run fail with a 403.

owl serve accepts writes only from its own address and from Vite on 127.0.0.1 or localhost, ports 5173 and 4173. If your web app runs anywhere else on your machine, name it:

owl serve --config probeowl --web-origin http://127.0.0.1:5180

Only loopback addresses are accepted: no other machine can use your owl serve.

docs.title: npm ci fails with EPERM
docs.text: On Windows, npm ci fails when another process holds files in web/node_modules, such as a Vite dev server still running, or another npm ci sharing npm's cache. Stop every Vite and Node process running from that folder, then run npm ci again. ProbeOwl's own merge checks use a separate install and cache, so they don't collide with yours.

docs.title: Oracle stops when idle (WSL)
docs.text:
The native Oracle runs in a WSL distribution, which WSL shuts down when nothing is using it. Keep it running in a window of its own:

bash dev/native/oracle_awake.sh

It starts the database if it's down, waits until FREEPDB1 is open, and holds the distribution awake until Ctrl-C.

docs.title: "takes no --config"
docs.text:
owl validate takes no --config: it runs through owl serve

owl validate, owl inspect, owl catalog import and owl kill are clients of owl serve, which already has the config. Start owl serve --config <folder>, then run the command without --config. See the CLI reference.

docs.title: A schema was never imported
docs.text:
The Tables screen, or saving a probe, says a connector's schema was never imported in an environment. Import it:

owl catalog import wallet_db --application wallet --env uat

Or use Import from replica on the Tables screen. The import reads tables, columns, keys and indexes, never data.

docs.title: "the store has no ProbeOwl tables yet" or "this release needs ..."
docs.text:
the store has no ProbeOwl tables yet; run: owl store init
the store schema is at <version>, this release needs <version>; run: owl store upgrade

owl serve needs ProbeOwl's own store, at this release's version:

owl store init          # creates ~/.probeowl/store.db, or upgrades an existing store

Set PROBEOWL_STORE_URL for a server database. A store on a network share is refused.

docs.title: "authentication failed"
docs.text:
authentication failed; check the binding's login and secret

The login or its password is wrong. Check the binding's user, and that its secret names an entry that exists:

uvx keyring get probeowl wallet_db.prod     # prints nothing if there's no such entry
uvx keyring set probeowl wallet_db.prod     # to save it again

no keychain entry for service 'probeowl' and user 'wallet_db.prod' means the entry is missing. On Linux without a desktop keychain, ProbeOwl refuses a keyring that keeps secrets in files. Use an env: secret instead.

docs.title: "connection refused"
docs.text:
the connection was refused or could not be made; check the database is up and the binding is right

The database isn't listening where the binding says. Check host and port, that the database is up, and that nothing blocks the port. Test connection on the Connectors screen tries again straight away.

docs.title: TLS: "could not be verified" or "could not be made over TLS"
docs.text: A server with a self-signed certificate fails verification. Install a certificate signed by a trusted authority, or, for a test server only, set trust_server_certificate: true with a trust_server_certificate_reason. A MariaDB or Oracle server that offers no TLS needs encrypt: false with an encrypt_reason. Production refuses either without a reason.

docs.title: Everything on a connector is Skipped
docs.text: The circuit breaker paused it because its replica is too far behind, or a kill switch is on. The run's reason says which, and the Connectors screen shows the pause or switch. See Safety.

docs.title: A record exists but ProbeOwl says Missing
docs.text: Production reads a replica, which can be behind. If the run carries the caveat "replica lag unknown", the login can't read the lag, so ProbeOwl can't tell a late record from a missing one. Grant the lag permission (Connectors), and Missing becomes Stale when the replica is too far behind.

docs.title: Writing probes
docs.text: This page builds the Wallet example's topup_completed probe from an empty file. A top-up completed when the provider captured the payment, sent its webhook, and the ledger posted one balanced double entry. The data lives in three systems: the wallet database (SQL Server), the payment provider's API, and the ledger (Oracle).

docs.title: 1. The entity: what a top-up is
docs.text:
An entity names the subject's root key and the identifiers that can find it:

# wallet/entities/topup.yaml
entity: topup
title: Top-up
root_key: topup_id
owner: payments-team

identifiers:
  topup_id: { pattern: '^tp_[0-9a-z]{6}$', unique: true }
  provider_payment_id: { pattern: '^pay_[0-9a-z]{6}$', via: record.provider_payment_id, unique: true }
  ledger_txn_id: { pattern: '^lt_[0-9a-z]{6}$', via: record.ledger_txn_id, unique: true }

via says where an identifier is looked up to find the root key, so a support agent can paste the provider's payment id instead of the top-up id. Patterns let ProbeOwl tell which one was typed. Add pii: true to an identifier such as an email, and it's masked wherever the run is shown.

docs.title: 2. Locations: where its data lives
docs.text:
locations:
  record:
    title: Top-up record
    using: wallet_db
    lookup: >
      SELECT id AS topup_id, user_id, amount, currency, status, provider_payment_id,
             ledger_txn_id, customer_email, created_at
      FROM topups WHERE id = :topup_id
    exposes: [topup_id, amount, currency, status, provider_payment_id, ledger_txn_id, created_at]
    pii: [customer_email]

  payment:
    title: Provider payment
    using: checkout_api
    key_from: record.provider_payment_id
    lookup: GET /payments/{{provider_payment_id}}
    fallback: GET /payments?reference={{topup_id}}
    exposes: [status, amount, currency]
    mask: [customer.email, customer.phone]

  webhook:
    title: Webhook deliveries
    using: wallet_db
    key_from: record.provider_payment_id
    lookup: >
      SELECT id, payment_id, event_type, received_at
      FROM provider_webhooks WHERE payment_id = :provider_payment_id
    cardinality: many
    max_rows: 20

  ledger:
    title: Ledger entries
    using: ledger_db
    key_from: record.ledger_txn_id
    lookup: >
      SELECT account, direction, amount, posted_at
      FROM ledger_entries WHERE txn_id = :ledger_txn_id
    cardinality: many
  • lookup is a single SELECT for a SQL connector, or GET <path> for a REST one. Keys are :parameters in SQL and {{name}} in a path, always bound, never pasted in.
  • key_from gives a location its key from another location's field. Here payment waits for record. If record.ledger_txn_id is empty, ledger is Blocked, and the empty link is reported: that's the finding.
  • fallback is tried when the lookup finds nothing, such as searching the provider by our own reference when the link was never saved.
  • exposes lists the fields other locations, identifiers and expectations may use.
  • pii (SQL columns) and mask (REST fields, as dotted paths) are masked in every result and in the evidence, before anything is stored. Columns the catalog marks as PII are masked too.
  • cardinality: many with max_rows for lists. The connector's row ceiling (default 1,000) is the most any lookup can return.
  • title is how the web app and the run header name it. Leave it out and the name is used, with spaces: ledger_entries becomes "Ledger entries".

docs.title: 3. Expectations: what must be true
docs.text:
# wallet/probes/topup_completed.yaml
probe: topup_completed
title: Top-up completed
kind: validate
entity: topup
owner: payments-team
description: A top-up was captured, confirmed by webhook and posted to the ledger once.
steps:
  - expect: record.status in ['succeeded', 'failed', 'pending']
  - expect:
      - payment.amount == record.amount
      - payment.currency == record.currency
  - expect: count(webhook) >= 1
  - when: record.status == 'succeeded'
    expect:
      - count(ledger) == 2
      - sum(ledger.amount where direction == 'credit')
        == sum(ledger.amount where direction == 'debit')
  - when: record.status == 'failed'
    expect:
      - record.ledger_txn_id == null
      - payment.status != 'captured'

The expression language:

You write It means record.status, payment.amount A field of a location's one record ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=, in [...], not in [...] Comparison, by meaning: 500, 500.00 and '500.00' are equal and, or, not, +, -, *, / As usual count(ledger), exists(ledger) How many rows; whether there are any sum(ledger.amount), min(...), max(...) Over a field of every row unique(cards.card_id) No value repeats all(cards, status == 'active'), any(...), none(...) Every, some or no row passes count(ledger where direction == 'credit') Only the rows that match now() The current time

Inside all, any, none and where, a bare name such as status is a field of that row. A fan-out location is read per row: all(cards, controller.status == status).

Steps run in order. A step with when: runs only when its condition holds; otherwise its expectations are skipped, which doesn't count against the run. A location that is Missing is seen only by count(), exists() and none(): anything else that reads it is skipped, and the skip fails the run. Use when: exists(refund) for a location that may be absent. See Concepts.

docs.title: 4. Save checks
docs.text:
The Probe editor checks a probe before it saves it, and owl check runs the same checks on a whole folder, except those that need a database:

  • Read-only: every lookup is a single SELECT (or WITH ... SELECT), with nothing that locks or writes.
  • Keyed or time-bounded: a lookup on a Transaction, Log or Audit table filters by a key or a bounded time window, so it never scans a growing table.
  • Index use: the query plan, read from the database, must seek an index, not scan the table. In Production, a login that can't read plans needs you to acknowledge that, and it's recorded.
  • PII masked: a column the catalog marks as PII, if a lookup selects it, is masked by that location's pii.
  • Row ceiling: no max_rows above the connector's ceiling.
  • Environments: every location's connector is bound where the probe may run.
  • Time offsets: a time with an offset is never compared with a column without one (see Connectors).

Each check shows what passed and why something didn't, with what to change. Saving shows the diff of the file before writing it.

docs.title: 5. Try it before saving
docs.text: Test run in the Probe editor runs your draft on a real ID, with the same guards and limits as any run. Its version starts with draft:, so it's never mistaken for the saved probe. When the result is what you expect, save.

docs.title: Inspect probes
docs.text:
An inspect probe has the same shape, with kind: inspect and usually a flat expect: list:

probe: visitor_cards
title: Visitor cards
kind: inspect
entity: visitor
owner: access-team
expect:
  - count(cards where status == 'active') <= 1
  - all(cards where status == 'active', valid_to > now())
  - all(cards, controller.status == status)

docs.title: Healthy comparison
docs.text: Give the entity a healthy_sample: an indexed SELECT of recent root keys that look healthy. Then a failed run can be compared, field by field, with the newest subject that passes the same probe. Fields marked expected_to_vary, such as an amount, are shown but never highlighted as a likely cause. The Wallet example's topup.yaml has one.

docs.title: Writing runbooks
docs.text: A runbook is the steps for a known problem, such as "top-up captured but wallet not credited". When a run finds that problem, the run suggests the runbook, and opening it from the run fills in the run's values. Runbooks live in git next to the probes, and are reviewed like code. This page follows examples/wallet/runbooks/topup_not_credited.yaml.

docs.title: Where a runbook goes
docs.text:
One runbook per file, in the application's folder, by convention under runbooks/:

probeowl/
  wallet/
    application.yaml
    connectors/
    entities/
    probes/
    runbooks/
      topup_not_credited.yaml

owl check <folder> checks it with the rest. To load a new or changed runbook into a running owl serve, use Reload configuration on the Connectors screen, or owl reload.

docs.title: The smallest runbook
docs.text:
# wallet/runbooks/topup_record_missing.yaml
runbook: topup_record_missing
title: record missing for a topup
application: wallet
applies_to: { entity: topup, when: [record.missing] }
owner: payments-team
last_verified: 2026-11-09
steps:
  - kind: manual
    id: check-the-source
    title: Check where the record should have been written
    text: Look the subject up in the system that writes it, and note what you find.
  - kind: probe
    id: check-again
    title: Check again after the fix
    probe: topup_completed

The Knowledge base offers one like it, built from your application's entity and probe, when the application has no runbooks yet.

Field What it is runbook Its id: a-z, 0-9 and _ title The symptom, as a person would search for it application The application it belongs to applies_to When a run suggests it: the entity, and when, a list of <location>.<outcome> owner The team that keeps it right last_verified When someone last checked that the steps still work steps What to do, in order: at least one

when names a location of the entity and an outcome: found, missing, waiting, blocked, ambiguous, error, stale or not_configured. [ledger.missing] is suggested by any run whose ledger location is Missing. List several to be suggested by any of them.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text: Each step has a kind, an id (a-z, 0-9 and -, unique in the runbook) and a title. Results, ticks and the audit key on the id, so keep it when you edit a step.

docs.title: Read query
docs.text:
- kind: read_query
    id: check-outbox
    title: Is the ledger posting stuck in the outbox?
    using: wallet_db
    sql: |
      SELECT TOP (20) id, status, attempts, last_error, created_at
      FROM outbox_events WHERE aggregate_id = :topup_id
      ORDER BY created_at DESC
    reviewed:
      by: s.khan
      date: 2026-10-12
      sql_sha256: 6cd2729de728c782f470a5978a49188ed078f281ef7afff7c41bf32a76b591ab

A single SELECT on one connector, with its values as :parameters filled in from the run. It can be run from the runbook, read-only and through the connector's guards, only when all of these hold:

  • it has a reviewed block;
  • its sql_sha256 matches the SQL exactly as it is now;
  • it passes the save checks, as a probe's lookup must.

Until then it's a reference query: shown, to copy, with the reason it can't run. Changing its SQL sends it back to reference only until it's reviewed again.

The reviewed block is added in the pull request where someone reviewed the query. owl runbook hash <file> prints each read query's sql_sha256, for that block. ProbeOwl never adds it itself.

docs.title: Write query
docs.text:
- kind: write_query
    id: requeue-posting
    title: Re-queue the ledger posting
    using: wallet_db
    requires: change approval; run by a DBA
    sql: |
      UPDATE outbox_events SET status = 'pending', attempts = 0
      WHERE aggregate_id = :topup_id AND status = 'failed'

A query that changes data. ProbeOwl never runs a write query. It shows it to copy, headed with where it applies and the approval it needs (requires), and records the copy in the audit. A read_query whose SQL changes data is shown as a write query too.

docs.title: External query
docs.text:
- kind: external_query
    id: ledger-errors
    title: Ledger service errors for this top-up
    tool: dynatrace
    query: |
      fetch logs
      | filter loglevel == "ERROR" and contains(content, :topup_id)
      | limit 100

A query for another tool, such as Dynatrace DQL, with the run's values filled in. Shown, to copy.

docs.title: Manual step
docs.text:
- kind: manual
    id: confirm-capture
    title: Confirm the capture in the provider dashboard
    text: Search the payment ID; check for a refund, dispute or partial capture.

A checkbox. Ticking it is saved with the run and audited.

docs.title: Probe
docs.text:
- kind: probe
    id: revalidate
    title: Re-validate after the fix
    probe: topup_completed

Runs a probe again on the run's subject, for example after a fix.

docs.title: Keeping runbooks right
docs.text:
A runbook is flagged Review due 90 days after its oldest reviewed read query was reviewed, or, with none, 90 days after last_verified. It's flagged Table drifted when a table one of its queries reads differs between the catalog and its latest schema import, or between environments: the Tables screen shows how. Check the steps, then update the dates in a pull request.

See Knowledge base for how runbooks look and run in the web app.

docs.title: Using the web app
docs.text:
The web app is ProbeOwl's main screen. It talks only to owl serve on your own machine.

Choose the application and the environment in the top bar. In Production, a red banner says so on every screen, and every run needs a reason and a reference. A kill switch that's on shows as a banner on every screen too.

Screen For Inspect A subject's current state, from any of its identifiers Validate Whether a flow ran correctly for one subject Probe editor Writing and testing probes, with the save checks Tables The table catalog: labels, marked columns, schema imports Connectors Each connector's health, role, lag and plan access Knowledge base Runbooks: the steps for a known problem, filled in from a run Compare files Two files side by side, masked (a tool)

Health (scheduled checks) and Runs (every investigation) are in the sidebar, but aren't built in this release. A run opens on the screen that started it, and the CLI prints its id.

docs.title: Compare files
docs.text:
Compare files is a tool, in the sidebar under Tools. It puts two files side by side, such as a provider's settlement file and your own export. It's a plugin, and can be turned off.

Choose two files. ProbeOwl lists every difference, field by field. Values that look like personal data are masked on screen and in the response, and are shown in full only from the file you chose, in your own browser.

docs.title: Connectors
docs.text:
Connectors shows each connector of the application in the chosen environment.

For each connector:

  • its type, and in Production its role under its name: Read replica, Readable secondary or Active Data Guard standby;
  • its limits: the row ceiling and statement timeout;
  • its replica lag, or why it's unknown, with the grant that would show it;
  • its plan access: whether the login can read query plans for the index check;
  • its status: healthy, paused by the circuit breaker, or stopped by a kill switch.

Test connection connects once, now, and says how long it took or why it failed. Hosts, logins and passwords never appear on this screen. To add a connector, see Connectors.

docs.title: Reload configuration
docs.text:
Reload configuration makes owl serve read its config folder again, so a connector, binding, entity or probe you added or changed is loaded without a restart. It says what it loaded and which applications and connectors changed, and it is recorded in the audit.

  • The folder is checked exactly as when owl serve starts. If it would refuse to start, nothing changes: what was loaded stays loaded, and the message says what is wrong (owl check <folder> lists every error).
  • It is refused while a run is running. Try again once it has finished.
  • Kill switches stay as they are: they're kept in the store, not in the folder. A switch on a connector you removed is still on if you add the connector back.
  • Plugins, the port, the store and the log file change only when owl serve is restarted.

owl reload does the same from the command line.

docs.title: Inspect
docs.text:
Inspect shows a subject's current state: everything an inspect probe reads about it, and which of its expectations fail.

  1. Choose the application and environment in the top bar.
  2. Type any identifier: a card id, a profile id, an email. ProbeOwl recognises it by its pattern, and says which one it detected.
  3. Give a reason, and in Production a reference, then Inspect.

The result:

  • Resolved shows how the identifier led to the subject: card_id C204518 → visitor_profile_id VP00012931, via cards.card_id.
  • Each one location is a card showing its record's fields. Each many location is a table, one row per record, with any fan-out lookup (here, the door controller) in its own column. Rows with a problem are highlighted, with the reason.
  • Expectations list each pass, fail and skip, with what was compared.
  • Evidence, per location, shows the exact query, parameters, guards and rows.
  • Copy command gives the owl inspect command that runs it again.

If the identifier finds several subjects, such as an email two visitors share, the run is Ambiguous: pick one, or Inspect both. Personal data stays masked throughout.

From a failed run, Compare with a healthy record and Suggested next steps work as they do on Validate.

docs.title: Knowledge base
docs.text:
The knowledge base holds runbooks: the steps for a known problem, such as "top-up captured but wallet not credited". They live in git next to the probes, and are reviewed like code.

A runbook's steps are of six kinds:

Step What ProbeOwl does with it Read query Runs it, read-only and through the guards, when the runbook is opened from a run: Run read-only Reference query Shows it, to copy Write query Shows it to copy, headed with where it applies and what it needs. Never run External query Shows it, to copy into another tool Manual step A checkbox to tick, recorded Probe Runs a probe again

Opened from a run (Open with values), each step's parameters are filled in from that run's values. A value that's masked, or that has no single value in the run, stays as :name, and that step can't run. Every run, copy and tick is audited.

To write one, see Writing runbooks.

docs.title: Probe editor
docs.text:
The Probe editor is where probes are written, checked and tested.

  • Open probe opens a saved probe; New probe starts a draft; New entity… builds an entity from the imported tables (below). On the left are its entity, kind, owner and the environments it's enabled in. In the middle, the YAML tab is the probe itself, Entity YAML is its entity, and Key graph shows how each location gets its key.
  • Check runs the save checks: expectations, environments, identifiers, read-only SQL, time filter and PII masking, and the index check against the database. Each says what passed, why something failed, and what would pass. See Writing probes.
  • Test run runs the draft on a real ID with every guard (Run draft). Its version starts with draft:.
  • Save first shows the change to the file as a diff, and confirming writes it. If the file changed since your preview, saving is refused and you preview again.

An existing probe opens as its real file: an edit changes only the lines you change, and keeps its comments.

docs.title: New entity
docs.text:
A probe checks one entity, so the first probe of a new subject type starts with New entity…. It builds the entity from the tables imported in the environment chosen in the top bar, on any SQL connector of the application, and reads no data. Import a connector's schema first, with Import from replica on the Tables screen.

  1. Name: the entity's id, title and owning team.
  2. Root table: the table one subject is a row of. Its primary key becomes the root key, which you can rename. A key named just id becomes <entity>_id.

  3. Locations: the other places the subject's data lives. Follow a key offers the tables, on any connector, that share a key with a location you've added:

    • a column the catalog links to another table (links_to), in either direction;
    • a column with the same distinctive name, such as provider_payment_id;
    • a column named for a table's key, such as cards.visitor_profile_id for visitor_profile.id.

    Common names, such as id, status, type, created_at or updated_at, are offered only when the catalog links them. To link on one yourself, use Link by columns…: pick a column of a location and a column of any imported table. A location whose key column is unique holds one record; otherwise it's many, with max_rows: 100, or the connector's row ceiling if that's lower. You choose the columns each location selects.

    Every location runs the save checks as soon as it's added, and a failure shows on that location, with its fix where the wizard knows one. The usual one: a Transaction, Log or Audit table may only be read by a key or within a time window, so cards read by visitor_profile_id fails until the catalog calls that column a link. Mark cards.visitor_profile_id as a link to visitor_profile.id previews that change to catalog.yaml, and Confirm in catalog.yaml writes it, as the Tables screen would. A failing location is never left out: fix it or remove it yourself. 4. Identifiers: what else can find a subject. Unique columns of a location keyed by the root key, such as cards.card_id, are ticked for you, with the reason. A unique column the catalog marks as PII, such as an email, is offered but not ticked; if you tick it, it's marked PII, so it stays masked. A pattern is optional. Only locations keyed by the root key are offered, since a value found there leads to its subject. 5. Preview: the YAML, then Check runs every save check on it, the index check included, and shows the new file as a diff. Create writes it.

The wizard only creates entities. To change one, open one of its probes and edit its Entity YAML, so the probes are checked with it. REST locations are written by hand: see Writing probes.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Tables is the table catalog: every table an application's probes and runbooks read, what kind of table it is, and which of its columns matter.

  • Import from replica reads a SQL connector's schema in one environment: tables, columns, keys, indexes and row estimates, never data. It does the same as owl catalog import.
  • Each table gets a suggested label: Transaction, Master, Audit, Log, Reference, External mapping or Outbox. The label sets defaults, such as needing a time window on tables that grow.
  • Mark column roles: primary key, time, status, link, external key, PII and compare.
  • A column named for another imported table's key is suggested as a link to it, on any connector: cards.visitor_profile_id links to visitor_profile.id, and topup_id to topups.id. A table on the same connector wins; two on other connectors are a guess, so neither is suggested. A link's target is picked from the imported tables and their columns, or typed with Other, not imported here…. A Transaction, Log or Audit table may be read by a link column, so marking it is what lets an entity look up rows by it.
  • Confirm writes the entry to the application's catalog.yaml, showing you the change first.
  • Alongside, it shows drift between environments, such as a column only UAT has, and which probes read each table.

docs.title: Validate
docs.text:
Validate checks that a flow ran correctly for one subject, such as a top-up being captured, confirmed by webhook and posted to the ledger.

  1. Choose the entity, type any ID it has (tp_91f2c7, or the provider's pay_7hq2m9), and choose the probe if there are several.
  2. Fill in the investigation record: a reason always, a reference in Production, and notes if they help. A customer reference is stored masked.
  3. Validate.

Locations fill in as they're read. Then:

  • First failure in dependency order names the first location that wasn't Found, or the first failed expectation. That's the place to start.
  • Locations list each outcome. Select one to see its evidence.
  • Expectations show pass, fail or skip, with the values compared, and why a step was skipped.
  • A run whose result may not be final, such as a Missing on a replica whose lag is unknown, carries a caveat on its status.

docs.title: Compare with a healthy record
docs.text: On a failed run, Compare with a healthy record runs the same probe on a known-good subject: the newest one that passes, a closer match such as Same payment method, or an ID you paste. Up to three candidates are tried, each one an audited run. The differences are listed field by field, likely causes first. Fields expected to vary, such as an amount, are shown but never highlighted.

docs.title: Suggested next steps
docs.text: Runbooks whose symptoms match the run's outcomes, such as "ledger missing", are suggested. Open with values opens one in the Knowledge base with the run's values filled in.
